Paper 3: The New Testament, Religion in Relation to Philosophy, Ethics and Morality, Historical Development of Islam (570CE-661CE). Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

The paper has six sections of six questions each: Section 2.1 The Gospel According to Luke (questions 1-6); Section 2.2 The Fourth Gospel (questions 7-12); Section 2.3 The Early Church as Reflected in Acts and 1 Corinthians (questions 13-18); Section 4.1 Philosophy of Religion (questions 19-24); Section 4.2 Ethics and Morality (questions 25-30); Section 6.0 The Historical Development of Islam (570CE - 661CE) (questions 31-36).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Analyse Jesus' doctrine of love and self-examination against the Jewish strict observance of the Law.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In the Fourth Gospel Jesus is often in conflict with Jewish leaders who insisted on strict observance of the Law, especially the Sabbath and the rules of purity. Against this, he teaches a doctrine centred on love and calls people to look honestly at themselves. This answer analyses these two ideas and sets them against the legal emphasis of his opponents.

**1. The Jewish strict observance of the Law.** For the Pharisees and other leaders the Law of Moses, with its Sabbath rules and purity regulations, defined the people of God. Obedience to the Law separated Israel from the nations. Some leaders applied it with great strictness, so that healing on the Sabbath counted as breaking the Law (John 5:9-16; 9:14-16).

**2. Jesus' doctrine of love.**
- Jesus gives a "new commandment": "love one another; as I have loved you" (John 13:34-35). Love is the mark by which others will know the disciples.
- He shows love in action by washing the disciples' feet (John 13:1-17) and by saying that there is no greater love than to lay down one's life for one's friends (John 15:12-13).
- The model of love is the love of the Father for the Son, and of Jesus for the disciples (John 15:9-10). Love and keeping his commands belong together (John 14:15, 21).
- His healings on the Sabbath are acts of love: the man at the pool (John 5) and the man born blind (John 9). He argues that if circumcision is performed on the Sabbath so that the Law of Moses is not broken, there is no reason to be angry that he made a man whole on the Sabbath (John 7:22-23).

**3. Self-examination.**
- The story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) has Jesus say, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone." Her accusers leave one by one. (Some manuscripts do not contain this passage, but it is traditionally printed at this place.) The strict application of the Law to others is checked by self-examination.
- After the healing of the blind man, Jesus says to the Pharisees who claim to see, "If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say 'We see', your guilt remains" (John 9:39-41).
- He tells those who study the Scriptures that these very Scriptures bear witness to him (John 5:39-47) and that they do not have the love of God in themselves (John 5:42).
- The leaders who refuse to enter Pilate's residence for fear of ritual defilement yet plot the death of Jesus (John 18:28) display the contradiction between outward observance and inner attitude.

**4. Assessment.** Jesus does not abolish the Law; the Prologue states that the Law was given through Moses and grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). He claims to fulfil it, and he moves the centre from outward observance to love and truth. His opponents regarded this as a threat to the Law, and this conflict led to their plot against him.

**Conclusion.** Strict observance stresses rules and outward correctness; Jesus stresses love and the honest examination of the heart. In John the real test of obedience to God is love of others, shown in the actions of Jesus himself.
